I have many cast iron pans and this is what I do:

Seasoning: This should be done when you buy a new pan or need to re-season a pan. I do this once every 7 or so years.

  • First, we want to remove the old or store bought seasoning, to do this: Coat the pan in a spray called 'hot shot'. This is an oven cleaner and very basic(as opposed to acidic). Place the pan in a sealed trash bag for 3-5 days and re-apply hot shot as necessary. Check once a day to see the status of the remaining seasoning.

  • Second, when the seasoning has been removed and you are only left with iron, rinse the pan and use vinegar to neutralize the hot shot. (If you see rust, you can use a rust remover solution or steel wool. Rust is your enemy.)

  • Third, heat the pan in the oven to 350 or so for 20-30 minutes. If I am feeling lazy, I just put the pan on the stove and heat it up real good.

  • Fourth, when the pan is nice and hot, use a bbq brush to coat the entire thing in coconut oil. Other oils work fine too but coconut has a higher smoke point so it is more likely to hold together at high temperatures. The pan oil should smoke a bit, that is ok.

  • Fifth, After cooling, wipe out extra oil and use the pan. Use water to clean for the first few uses. The oil will build up over time to create a new seasoning.

Whatever your preferred oil is, look up its smoke point. This is the temperature that your oil of choice starts to burn at. Keep your pan below that temperature when cooking so your season lasts as long as possible. Stove-top cooking will not heat the pan above the temperature of the food, especially if there's a good amount of water, fat, or oil in the pan, thanks to heat transfer. Ovens will obviously not heat above what you set it at. If your chosen oil's smoke point is noticeably low, you might want to consider picking one with a higher smoke point.

Personally, I have two pans, one for stove-top and one for the oven (if the recipe requires going from the stove to the oven, which is a lot, I just use the oven pan the whole time). The stove-top pan I season with cold-pressed extra virgin olive oil, for flavor and simplicity, as that's the oil I use in most of my cooking (half-Italian, quarter-French). For the oven pan I use, believe it or not, clarified butter. Clarified butter does not go rancid like regular butter, and has a rather high smoke point (above 450), so it won't burn in the oven.

The first thing about cast iron is understanding what seasoning actually is. It's a polymerized layer of fat that acts as a protective semi non-stick coating. This is accomplished by heating fat, typically a cooking oil, on the surface of the cast iron beyond its smoke point until it polymerizes. This coating is not teflon nor will it ever be perfect so you're not going to want to expose it to water for extended periods of time like soaking it in the sink and acidic foods will eat through it. Cast iron is porous so avoid cooking seafood with cast iron unless you want everything to taste like fish, this is also the reason you never want to use soap on cast iron unless you're completely re-seasoning it. Also, oiling it is not seasoning it, seasoning it requires heat for polymerization.

What condition is it in? If it's rusty you're basically going to need to start over by removing everything from all surfaces (including the handle) with steel wool or some sort of very abrasive metal brush, water, and if you want soap. The goal here is to strip all of the seasoning, rust, and everything else. This is the only time you should ever even consider using soap on cast iron. Soap is never needed on properly seasoned cast iron. Dry it thoroughly, place it on a burner until all of the water has evaporated, then allow it to cool. Next you'll want to season it by lightly and evenly coating all surfaces with oil then put it in the oven upside down at a temperature higher than the oils smoke point for an hour. Basically turn your oven on the highest setting, but any temperature above the smoke point should work. Place a foil lined baking sheet below it to catch any oil drips. Expect it to smoke, if it doesn't the temperature is too low. Let it cool, then inspect it for any uneven areas in the seasoning. All surfaces, most importantly the cooking surfaces, should have a bit of a shine to them you're aiming for semi-gloss. If the seasoning is uneven put another coat of oil on it and repeat the oven steps, if any part is sticky repeat the oven step.

If it's in good condition you will want to wash it after every use with water and a sponge, spatula, or a non-metal brush. If anything is stuck on it you can clean it by heating it back up then run hot water over it in the sink and hit it with a wood spatula, avoid plastic tools as they can melt. You can also use warm water and salt with a sponge. Dry it completely by placing it on a burner until all of the water has evaporated. This step is important, you don't want it to rust. Some will tell you to oil it after it cools, but I personally avoid this since the oil is going to act like a magnet for any dust in the air, besides you're probably going to oil it when you cook with it next. However, if you're in a humid climate you'll probably want to oil it to protect from rust. Inspect it, it should be semi-gloss, if it's not you probably need to re-season it. If it needs a re-seasoning repeat the steps in the second paragraph, but skip the steps that remove the seasoning.

Now on to what oil should you use. Lard is the traditional fat used to season cast iron, but basically most food grade fats/oils will work. Popular choices are vegetable oil, canola oil, and shortening.
